subject: maths

moments.title: Turing's universal machine
moments.body:
Turing, age 24, publishes 'On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem'. He defines a mathematical model of computation — what we now call a Turing machine — and proves the halting problem undecidable.

The universal Turing machine reads its own description from a tape: a single machine can simulate any other. This is the theoretical basis of every programmable computer.
moments.takeaway: Computation has a mathematical foundation. Programmable computers are theoretically possible before they exist.

moments.title: Bletchley Park and the Enigma
moments.who: Alan Turing, Gordon Welchman, others — Bletchley Park, Buckinghamshire
moments.body:
Turing is recruited to Bletchley Park to break the German Enigma cipher. He extends Polish work and designs the Bombe — an electromechanical device that searches for the daily Enigma key by exhaustive testing of possibilities.

Later, Turing's work on the Lorenz cipher (used by Hitler's high command) leads Tommy Flowers to build Colossus — arguably the first electronic programmable computer.

The work was kept secret for 30 years. Estimates suggest it shortened WWII by 2 to 4 years and saved millions of lives.
moments.takeaway: Turing's theoretical work becomes life-saving wartime engineering — and stays classified for decades.

moments.title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
moments.body:
Turing publishes 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' in the philosophy journal Mind. He asks: can machines think?

He proposes the imitation game (Turing test): if a machine can convince a human judge that it's a human in conversation, we should agree it 'thinks'. He predicts a 70 percent success rate within 50 years. He underestimates the difficulty — but the conceptual frame is still used today.

quote.text: The original question, 'Can machines think?' I believe to be too meaningless to deserve discussion.

moments.takeaway: Turing recasts the question of machine intelligence as a behavioural test.

moments.title: Turing convicted of gross indecency
moments.body:
Turing reports a burglary at his Manchester home and incidentally reveals his relationship with another man to the police. Homosexual acts are illegal in Britain. Turing is prosecuted, convicted, and sentenced to chemical castration (oestrogen injections) as an alternative to prison.

The injections cause physical and psychological side effects. He loses his security clearance.
moments.takeaway: One of the most important figures of the 20th century is destroyed by the laws of his own country.

moments.title: Turing's death
moments.body:
Turing is found dead in his bed by his housekeeper, on 8 June 1954. Cause of death: cyanide poisoning. A half-eaten apple lies beside him.

The inquest rules suicide. His mother believed it was an accident from his amateur chemistry experiments. He was 41.

The British government formally apologised in 2009 (Gordon Brown) and pardoned him posthumously in 2013. The 'Alan Turing Law' (2017) pardoned other men convicted under the same legislation.
moments.takeaway: The mathematical father of the computer dies at 41 by his own hand, after the state he helped save destroyed his career and health.

now.title: Computation today
now.body:
Computers run our civilisation. Turing's universal machine is the conceptual ancestor of every modern device. The theoretical limits he identified (halting problem, undecidability) constrain modern computer science.

AI now passes some versions of the Turing test for short conversations. Large language models can write code, do mathematics, hold conversations. Whether they 'think' is a question Turing predicted we would have to face.
now.open_questions: Will quantum computers break classical limits? (For some problems, yes — Shor's algorithm factors integers fast.) What is consciousness, and could a computer have it? How do we govern AI systems that can outperform humans on many cognitive tasks?

reflection: Turing's contribution to defeating Nazi Germany was central, his contribution to modern computing was foundational, and his work on biological pattern formation (1952, on morphogenesis) was pioneering. Yet he died in shame, criminalised by his own government. How does a society make amends for state-sanctioned destruction of its own creative minds? How does it prevent the next one?
